claim: Nociceptive habituation is a conserved process through which pain sensitivity threshold is adjusted based on past sensory experience.
source: Nociceptive habituation is a conserved process through which pain sensitivity threshold is adjusted based on past sensory experience and which may be dysregulated in human chronic pain conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nociceptive habituation without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Nociceptive habituation may be dysregulated in human chronic pain conditions.
source: Nociceptive habituation is a conserved process through which pain sensitivity threshold is adjusted based on past sensory experience and which may be dysregulated in human chronic pain conditions.
evidence: This is presented as speculative reasoning about the relevance to human disease.

claim: Noxious heat habituation in Caenorhabditis elegans involves the nuclear translocation of CaM kinase-1 (CMK-1) in the FLP thermo-nociceptors neurons.
source: Noxious heat habituation in Caenorhabditis elegans involves the nuclear translocation of CaM kinase-1 (CMK-1) in the FLP thermo-nociceptors neurons, causing reduced animal heat sensitivity and avoidance responses.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies and experimental observations in this manuscript.

claim: Nuclear translocation of CMK-1 in FLP neurons causes reduced animal heat sensitivity and avoidance responses.
source: Noxious heat habituation in Caenorhabditis elegans involves the nuclear translocation of CaM kinase-1 (CMK-1) in the FLP thermo-nociceptors neurons, causing reduced animal heat sensitivity and avoidance responses.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The phosphorylation of CMK-1 on T179 by CaM kinase kinase-1 (CKK-1) is required for nuclear entry.
source: The phosphorylation of CMK-1 on T179 by CaM kinase kinase-1 (CKK-1) is required for nuclear entry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this manuscript and previous studies.

claim: A specific nuclear export sequence (NES) is required to maintain CMK-1 in the cytoplasm at rest (20°C).
source: Recently, we identified a specific nuclear export sequence (NES) required to maintain CMK-1 in the cytoplasm at rest (20°C) and showed that Ca2+/CaM binding is sufficient to enhance CMK-1 affinity for IMA-3 via a specific nuclear localization signal (NLS) in order to promote nuclear entry after persistent heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C) (Ippolito et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: Ca2+/CaM binding is sufficient to enhance CMK-1 affinity for IMA-3 via a specific nuclear localization signal (NLS).
source: Recently, we identified a specific nuclear export sequence (NES) required to maintain CMK-1 in the cytoplasm at rest (20°C) and showed that Ca2+/CaM binding is sufficient to enhance CMK-1 affinity for IMA-3 via a specific nuclear localization signal (NLS) in order to promote nuclear entry after persistent heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C) (Ippolito et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: Ca2+/CaM binding promotes CMK-1 nuclear entry after persistent heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C).
source: Recently, we identified a specific nuclear export sequence (NES) required to maintain CMK-1 in the cytoplasm at rest (20°C) and showed that Ca2+/CaM binding is sufficient to enhance CMK-1 affinity for IMA-3 via a specific nuclear localization signal (NLS) in order to promote nuclear entry after persistent heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C) (Ippolito et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: Additional functional NES and NLS on CMK-1 can counteract previously identified elements.
source: Here, we identified additional functional NES and NLS on CMK-1, whose activity can counteract previously identified elements.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claim: T179 phosphorylation can promote nuclear entry both downstream of CaM binding and as part of an independent/parallel pathway.
source: T179 phosphorylation can promote nuclear entry both downstream of CaM binding and as part of an independent/parallel pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claim: T179 phosphorylation can promote nuclear export.
source: Moreover, T179 phosphorylation can also produce the opposite effect by promoting nuclear export.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claim: Multiple calcium-dependent regulatory mechanisms converge to bias the activity pattern across a network of NES/NLS elements to control CMK-1 nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling.
source: Taken together, our studies suggest that multiple calcium-dependent regulatory mechanisms converge to bias the activity pattern across a network of NES/NLS elements, in order to control CMK-1 nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling, and actuate stimulation-dependent nociceptive plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+/CaM-dependent protein kinases (CaMK) are conserved effectors of the universal calcium second messenger.
source: Ca2+/CaM-dependent protein kinases (CaMK) are conserved effectors of the universal calcium second messenger, mediating important plasticity effects in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CaMKs.

claim: CaMKs mediate important plasticity effects in the nervous system.
source: Ca2+/CaM-dependent protein kinases (CaMK) are conserved effectors of the universal calcium second messenger, mediating important plasticity effects in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CaMKs.

claim: CaMKs phosphorylate diverse intracellular substrates in response to neuronal activation to actuate changes in cell physiology.
source: In response to neuronal activation, these kinases phosphorylate diverse intracellular substrates in order to actuate changes in cell physiology (Soderling, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soderling, 1999.

claim: CaMKI includes an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain.
source: CaMKI includes an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain, which inhibits its catalytic activity (Goldberg et al., 1996; Hook and Means, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 1996 and Hook and Means, 2001.

claim: The C-terminal regulatory domain of CaMKI inhibits its catalytic activity.
source: CaMKI includes an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain, which inhibits its catalytic activity (Goldberg et al., 1996; Hook and Means, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 1996 and Hook and Means, 2001.

claim: CaMKI auto-inhibition is released upon binding of Ca2+/CaM in the regulatory domain.
source: This auto-inhibition is released upon binding of Ca2+/CaM in the regulatory domain and the kinase can be fully activated after phosphorylation of a specific threonine in the activation loop (T177 in human) by CaMK kinase I (CaMKKI).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaMKI regulation.

claim: CaMKI can be fully activated after phosphorylation of T177 (in human) by CaMKKI.
source: This auto-inhibition is released upon binding of Ca2+/CaM in the regulatory domain and the kinase can be fully activated after phosphorylation of a specific threonine in the activation loop (T177 in human) by CaMK kinase I (CaMKKI).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaMKI regulation.

claim: In mammals, CaM binding on CaMKI is a prerequisite prior to the phosphorylation of T177.
source: In mammals, CaM binding on CaMKI is a prerequisite prior to the phosphorylation of T177.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian CaMKI regulation.

claim: The Caenorhabditis elegans CaMKI (named CMK-1) displays similar structural and functional properties to mammalian CaMKI.
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans CaMKI (named CMK-1) displays similar structural and functional properties, with a conserved activation loop threonine (T179 in the worm sequence) (Eto et al., 1999; Kimura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eto et al., 1999 and Kimura et al., 2002.

claim: C. elegans CMK-1 has a conserved activation loop threonine at position T179.
source: The Caenorhabditis elegans CaMKI (named CMK-1) displays similar structural and functional properties, with a conserved activation loop threonine (T179 in the worm sequence) (Eto et al., 1999; Kimura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eto et al., 1999 and Kimura et al., 2002.

claim: CMK-1 mediates multiple plasticity mechanisms, including during salt aversive learning, habituation to repeated mechanical stimulations, and thermal adaptation to innocuous and noxious heat.
source: CMK-1 mediates multiple plasticity mechanisms, including during salt aversive learning, habituation to repeated mechanical stimulations, and thermal adaptation to innocuous and noxious heat (Ardiel et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2018; Neal et al., 2015; Satterlee et al., 2004; Schild et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The subcellular localization of CMK-1 can be regulated in a stimulus-dependent manner in different contexts.
source: The subcellular localization of CMK-1 can be regulated in a stimulus-dependent manner in different contexts (Moss et al., 2016; Neal et al., 2015; Schild et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CMK-1 activity in the cytoplasm promotes heat avoidance response in FLP neurons.
source: Previous experiments conducted in transgenic animals expressing different CMK-1 mutants in FLP with constitutive nuclear or cytoplasmic localization notably showed that CMK-1 activity in the cytoplasm promotes heat avoidance response, while its activity in the nucleus acts antagonistically to reduce heat avoidance response (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: CMK-1 activity in the nucleus acts antagonistically to reduce heat avoidance response in FLP neurons.
source: Previous experiments conducted in transgenic animals expressing different CMK-1 mutants in FLP with constitutive nuclear or cytoplasmic localization notably showed that CMK-1 activity in the cytoplasm promotes heat avoidance response, while its activity in the nucleus acts antagonistically to reduce heat avoidance response (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: In wild type worms exposed to innocuous temperature (20°C), CMK-1 resides mostly in the FLP cytoplasm.
source: In wild type worms exposed to innocuous temperature (20°C), CMK-1 resides mostly in the FLP cytoplasm, where it promotes high sensitivity to heat and robust avoidance responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in this and previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic CMK-1 promotes high sensitivity to heat and robust avoidance responses.
source: In wild type worms exposed to innocuous temperature (20°C), CMK-1 resides mostly in the FLP cytoplasm, where it promotes high sensitivity to heat and robust avoidance responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization and functional data.

claim: Upon persistent noxious heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C) CMK-1 progressively translocates in the nucleus.
source: Upon persistent noxious heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C) CMK-1 progressively translocates in the nucleus, where it acts to reduce the animal heat sensitivity and dampen avoidance responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this and previous studies.

claim: Nuclear CMK-1 acts to reduce the animal heat sensitivity and dampen avoidance responses.
source: Upon persistent noxious heat stimulation (90 min at 28°C) CMK-1 progressively translocates in the nucleus, where it acts to reduce the animal heat sensitivity and dampen avoidance responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization and functional data.

claim: NES288-294 is a canonical nuclear export sequence of CMK-1 located immediately adjacent to the CaM-binding domain in the regulatory domain.
source: First, the NES288-294 canonical nuclear export sequence of CMK-1, located immediately adjacent to the CaM-binding domain in the regulatory domain and representing a major determinant of CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization at 20°C.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: NES288-294 represents a major determinant of CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization at 20°C.
source: First, the NES288-294 canonical nuclear export sequence of CMK-1, located immediately adjacent to the CaM-binding domain in the regulatory domain and representing a major determinant of CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization at 20°C.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: NLS71-78 is a canonical nuclear localization sequence located on the N-terminal catalytic domain of CMK-1.
source: Second, the NLS71-78 canonical nuclear localization sequence, located on the N-terminal catalytic domain of CMK-1, and which can interact with IMA-3 importin in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: NLS71-78 can interact with IMA-3 importin in vitro.
source: Second, the NLS71-78 canonical nuclear localization sequence, located on the N-terminal catalytic domain of CMK-1, and which can interact with IMA-3 importin in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: The binding of Ca2+/CaM on CMK-1 can strengthen its interaction with IMA-3 importin via NLS71-78.
source: We furthermore showed that the binding of Ca2+/CaM on CMK-1 can strengthen its interaction with IMA-3 importin via NLS71-78 (Ippolito et al., 2021), constituting a calcium-dependent mechanism through which thermosensory activity causes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Ippolito et al., 2021).

claim: Ca2+/CaM binding constitutes a calcium-dependent mechanism through which thermosensory activity causes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
source: We furthermore showed that the binding of Ca2+/CaM on CMK-1 can strengthen its interaction with IMA-3 importin via NLS71-78 (Ippolito et al., 2021), constituting a calcium-dependent mechanism through which thermosensory activity causes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data cited.

claim: A T179A mutation on CMK-1 can decrease CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C.
source: Indeed, a T179A mutation on CMK-1 as well as a null mutation in the ckk-1 gene can both decrease CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: A null mutation in the ckk-1 gene can decrease CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C.
source: Indeed, a T179A mutation on CMK-1 as well as a null mutation in the ckk-1 gene can both decrease CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: The NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant is slightly enriched in the nucleus at 20°C.
source: This double mutant is slightly enriched in the nucleus at 20°C and translocates in the cytoplasm at 28°C, corresponding to a reverted behavior as compared to wild type CMK-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant translocates in the cytoplasm at 28°C.
source: This double mutant is slightly enriched in the nucleus at 20°C and translocates in the cytoplasm at 28°C, corresponding to a reverted behavior as compared to wild type CMK-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant displays reverted behavior as compared to wild type CMK-1.
source: This double mutant is slightly enriched in the nucleus at 20°C and translocates in the cytoplasm at 28°C, corresponding to a reverted behavior as compared to wild type CMK-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the double mutant behavior to wild type.

claim: A secondary pair of antagonistic NES/NLS determinants becomes predominant when NES288-294/NLS71-78-dependent pathways are deactivated.
source: The simplest explanation for this behavior would involve a secondary pair of antagonistic NES/NLS determinants, whose activity becomes predominant only when the major drives (NES288-294/NLS71-78 -dependent pathways) are deactivated.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the double mutant.

claim: Impairing the NLS297-307 element with a K307Q mutation in the NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant background fully blocked its nuclear accumulation at 20°C.
source: We found that impairing the NLS297-307 element with a K307Q mutation in the NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant background fully blocked its nuclear accumulation at 20°C (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The K307Q mutation could reinforce the cytoplasmic enrichment at 28°C in the NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant background.
source: This mutation could also reinforce the cytoplasmic enrichment at 28°C (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The NLS297-307-dependent nuclear entry pathway contributes to translocate CMK-1 in the nucleus, independently of the NLS71-78/NES288-294 pair.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the NLS297-307-dependent nuclear entry pathway contributes to translocate CMK-1 in the nucleus, independently of the NLS71-78/NES288-294 pair.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on the K307Q mutation.

claim: The NLS71-78; NES288-294; NES315-323 triple mutant protein could still be exported from the nucleus.
source: We found that the NLS71-78; NES288-294; NES315-323 triple mutant protein could still be exported from the nucleus, like the NLS71-78; NES288-294 double (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The candidate NES315-323 sequence does not mediate CMK-1 nuclear export in any of the conditions examined.
source: Therefore, the candidate NES315-323 sequence does not mediate CMK-1 nuclear export in any of the conditions examined so far across our studies.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of the NES315-323 mutation.

claim: A CMK-1 (1–304) mutant was previously shown to accumulate in the nucleus.
source: Indeed, a CMK-1 (1–304) mutant was previously shown to accumulate in the nucleus and proposed to lack some NES located in the 305–348 region (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: CMK-1 (1–304) mutant was proposed to lack some NES located in the 305–348 region.
source: Indeed, a CMK-1 (1–304) mutant was previously shown to accumulate in the nucleus and proposed to lack some NES located in the 305–348 region (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: An S325A mutation produced a partial yet significant reduction in heat stimulus-evoked nuclear export when introduced in the NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant background.
source: We found that an S325A mutation produced a partial yet significant reduction in heat stimulus-evoked nuclear export when introduced in the NLS71-78; NES288-294 double mutant background (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The single S325A mutant displayed a significantly more nuclear localization at both 20°C and 28°C as compared to CMK-1(wt).
source: Furthermore, as compared to CMK-1(wt), the single S325A mutant displayed a significantly more nuclear localization at both 20°C and 28°C (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A double mutant protein combining S325A and NES288-294 mutations markedly accumulated in the nucleus at both temperatures.
source: A double mutant protein combining S325A and NES288-294 mutations markedly accumulated in the nucleus at both temperatures, reaching nuclear/cytoplasmic signal ratio values significantly higher than that of any single mutation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Serine 325 is part of a functional element promoting CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization.
source: Therefore, serine 325 is part of a functional element promoting CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization and regulating CMK-1 localization independently of NES288-294.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on S325 mutations.

claim: Serine 325 regulates CMK-1 localization independently of NES288-294.
source: Therefore, serine 325 is part of a functional element promoting CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization and regulating CMK-1 localization independently of NES288-294.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on S325 mutations.

claim: The S325D mutant localization was the same as wild type.
source: Consistent with this view, the S325D mutant localization was the same as wild type (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: An intact S325 residue is necessary for the normal nuclear export of CMK-1(wt).
source: These observations suggest (i) that an intact S325 residue is necessary for the normal nuclear export of CMK-1(wt) and (ii) that S325 phosphorylation might be the default state of CMK-1 in FLP under our conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on S325 mutations.

claim: S325 phosphorylation might be the default state of CMK-1 in FLP under the experimental conditions.
source: These observations suggest (i) that an intact S325 residue is necessary for the normal nuclear export of CMK-1(wt) and (ii) that S325 phosphorylation might be the default state of CMK-1 in FLP under our conditions.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: The post-translational modification of S325 could be used as a regulatory switch to control CMK-1 localization.
source: Our data also suggest that the post-translational modification of S325 could be used as a regulatory switch to control CMK-1 localization.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: S325 promotes CMK-1 cytoplasmic accumulation independently of NES288-294.
source: We know that S325 promotes CMK-1 cytoplasmic accumulation independently of NES288-294 (as shown by the impact of the S325A mutation in a NES288-294 mutant background Figure 1D and E), but how the S325-element works remains to be determined.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The S325-element could function by promoting a non-canonical nuclear export or a cytoplasmic retention pathway.
source: In principle, it could either function by promoting a non-canonical nuclear export or a cytoplasmic retention pathway, for example, by anchoring CMK-1 to some cytoplasmic components.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: S325 phosphorylation/dephosphorylation modifications are not involved in the heat-evoked CMK-1 re-localization process in FLP.
source: Furthermore, it seems that S325 phosphorylation/dephosphorylation modifications are not involved in the heat-evoked CMK-1 re-localization process in FLP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The S325 phosphorylation mechanism might be relevant in other contexts in FLP and/or in other neuron types.
source: However, we speculate that this mechanism might be relevant in other contexts in FLP and/or in other neuron types.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about possible broader relevance.

claim: At 20°C, the strong NLS71-78-dependent nuclear entry pathway is inactive.
source: At 20°C, the strong NLS71-78 -dependent nuclear entry pathway is inactive and the activity of the weaker NLS297-307 pathway is over-competed by both NES288-294-dependent and the S325-dependent export pathways, which are both active.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a working model.

claim: At 20°C, the activity of the weaker NLS297-307 pathway is over-competed by both NES288-294-dependent and the S325-dependent export pathways.
source: At 20°C, the strong NLS71-78 -dependent nuclear entry pathway is inactive and the activity of the weaker NLS297-307 pathway is over-competed by both NES288-294-dependent and the S325-dependent export pathways, which are both active.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a working model.

claim: At 28°C, the strong NLS71-78-dependent nuclear entry pathway is active and is the main drive to shift the equilibrium toward the nucleus.
source: At 28°C, the strong NLS71-78-dependent nuclear entry pathway is active and is the main drive to shift the equilibrium toward the nucleus, even if the other elements might still be active.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a working model.

claim: A phosphorylation-dead CMK-1(T179A) mutant protein displays impaired activity-dependent nuclear accumulation.
source: Previous studies have shown that a phosphorylation-dead CMK-1(T179A) mutant protein displays impaired activity-dependent nuclear accumulation (Schild et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schild et al., 2014 and Yu et al., 2014.

claim: The T179A mutation left CMK-1 reporter localization unchanged in FLP at 20°C.
source: Indeed, while the T179A mutation left CMK-1 reporter localization unchanged in FLP at 20°C, it abolished its nuclear accumulation after 90 min of cell activation at 28°C (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: The T179A mutation abolished CMK-1 nuclear accumulation after 90 min of cell activation at 28°C.
source: Indeed, while the T179A mutation left CMK-1 reporter localization unchanged in FLP at 20°C, it abolished its nuclear accumulation after 90 min of cell activation at 28°C (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: The ability of CMK-1 to be phosphorylated on T179 is essential for its activity-dependent nuclear translocation.
source: Hence, we confirm that the ability of CMK-1 to be phosphorylated on T179 is essential for its activity-dependent nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on the T179A mutation.

claim: The unc-68(dom13) mutation chronically elevates FLP cytoplasmic calcium levels at both 20°C and 28°C.
source: To confirm that T179-dependent nuclear accumulation indeed takes place downstream of calcium elevation, we tested if the T179A mutation could block the effect of the unc-68(dom13) mutation, which chronically elevates FLP cytoplasmic calcium levels at both 20°C and 28°C to promote CMK-1 nuclear accumulation (Figure 2A; Ippolito et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ippolito et al., 2021 and Marques et al., 2019.

claim: The unc-68(dom13) mutation promotes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
source: To confirm that T179-dependent nuclear accumulation indeed takes place downstream of calcium elevation, we tested if the T179A mutation could block the effect of the unc-68(dom13) mutation, which chronically elevates FLP cytoplasmic calcium levels at both 20°C and 28°C to promote CMK-1 nuclear accumulation (Figure 2A; Ippolito et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ippolito et al., 2021 and Marques et al., 2019.

claim: The CMK-1 nuclear accumulation caused by the unc-68(dom13) mutation was fully abolished by the T179A mutation at either temperature.
source: The CMK-1 nuclear accumulation caused by the unc-68(dom13) mutation was fully abolished by the T179A mutation at either temperature (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The phosphorylation of T179 mediates the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1 downstream of Ca2+ elevation, irrespective of the temperature.
source: We conclude that the phosphorylation of T179 mediates the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1 downstream of Ca2+ elevation, irrespective of the temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179A and unc-68(dom13) interactions.

claim: T179A and W305S mutations alone or in combination had little impact on the cytoplasmic localization of CMK-1 at 20°C.
source: Each of these mutations alone or in combination had little impact on the cytoplasmic localization of CMK-1 at 20°C (Figure 2D, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At 28°C, the single T179A and W305S mutations as well as the combined mutations fully prevented the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1.
source: At 28°C, the single mutations as well as the combined mutations had a similar effect, fully preventing the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1, with ratio values similar to the situation at 20°C (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The lack of a cumulative effect between T179A and W305S mutations suggests that CaM binding and T179 phosphorylation might be part of the same pathway.
source: Whereas we cannot rule out a floor effect in the ratio measure, the lack of a cumulative effect between the two mutations suggests that CaM binding and T179 phosphorylation might be part of the same pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on the double mutant.

claim: T179 phosphorylation acts downstream of intracellular calcium elevation and CaM binding to regulate cell activity-dependent CMK-1 nuclear entry.
source: Collectively, these results are consistent with a model in which T179 phosphorylation acts downstream of intracellular calcium elevation and CaM binding to regulate cell activity-dependent CMK-1 nuclear entry.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data presented.

claim: The T179D phospho-mimicking mutation can favor nuclear accumulation in the absence of thermal stimulation at 20°C.
source: To address this question, we examined the impact of the T179D phospho-mimicking mutation at 20°C and found it could favor nuclear accumulation in the absence of thermal stimulation (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: T179 phosphorylation directly contributes to trigger CMK-1(wt) nuclear accumulation at 28°C.
source: Therefore, whereas T179 phosphorylation directly contribute to trigger CMK-1(wt) nuclear accumulation at 28°C, additional mechanisms are likely to occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D.

claim: Additional mechanisms beyond T179 phosphorylation are likely to contribute to CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C.
source: Therefore, whereas T179 phosphorylation directly contribute to trigger CMK-1(wt) nuclear accumulation at 28°C, additional mechanisms are likely to occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D.

claim: At 20°C, the T179D mutation can favor CMK-1 nuclear localization in a W305S mutant background abolishing CaM binding.
source: At 20°C, the T179D mutation could also favor CMK-1 nuclear localization in a W305S mutant background abolishing CaM binding (Figure 3B; two-way ANOVA: main effect of T179D, p<0.001; main effect of W305S, p<0.001, T179D × W305S interaction, p=0.637).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The T179D phosphomimic mutation is sufficient to promote CMK-1 nuclear accumulation independently of CaM binding at 20°C.
source: Thus, the T179D phosphomimic mutation is sufficient to promote CMK-1 nuclear accumulation independently of CaM binding at 20°C, suggesting that T179 phosphorylation functions either downstream of CaM binding or in a separate pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D and W305S interactions.

claim: T179 phosphorylation functions either downstream of CaM binding or in a separate pathway.
source: Thus, the T179D phosphomimic mutation is sufficient to promote CMK-1 nuclear accumulation independently of CaM binding at 20°C, suggesting that T179 phosphorylation functions either downstream of CaM binding or in a separate pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D and W305S interactions.

claim: The W305S mutation produced a small cytoplasmic translocation effect in both wild type and T179D backgrounds.
source: Interestingly, our data also show that the W305S mutation produced a small cytoplasmic translocation effect in both wild type and T179D backgrounds (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CaM binding can increase CMK-1 affinity for IMA-3 in an in vitro context devoid of CKK-1 and of T179 phosphorylation.
source: These observations are compatible with the results of our previous protein interaction analyses, having shown that CaM binding can increase CMK-1 affinity for IMA-3 in an in vitro context devoid of CKK-1 and of T179 phosphorylation (Ippolito et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ippolito et al., 2021.

claim: CaM binding promotes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation through a direct pathway by reinforcing the interaction between IMA-3 and the NLS71-78 element of CMK-1.
source: The simplest model explaining these results would involve two mechanisms through which CaM binding promotes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation: (i) a direct pathway, through which CaM binding reinforces the interaction between IMA-3 and the NLS71-78 element of CMK-1 and (ii) an indirect pathway, through which CaM binding is required prior to phosphorylation of T179, which in turn promotes the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: CaM binding promotes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation through an indirect pathway where CaM binding is required prior to phosphorylation of T179.
source: The simplest model explaining these results would involve two mechanisms through which CaM binding promotes CMK-1 nuclear accumulation: (i) a direct pathway, through which CaM binding reinforces the interaction between IMA-3 and the NLS71-78 element of CMK-1 and (ii) an indirect pathway, through which CaM binding is required prior to phosphorylation of T179, which in turn promotes the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: T179A markedly promoted CMK-1 cytoplasmic retention at 28°C regardless of the NES288-294 mutation.
source: We found that T179A markedly promoted CMK-1 cytoplasmic retention at 28°C regardless of the NES288-294 mutation (Figure 3C, two-way ANOVA: main effect of T179A, p<0.001; main effect of NES288-294, p<0.001, T179A × NES288-294 interaction, p=0.384).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: It is unlikely that the T179A mutation predominantly causes CMK-1 cytoplasmic translocation by aberrantly revealing NES288-294 at 28°C.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that the T179A mutation predominantly causes CMK-1 cytoplasmic translocation by aberrantly revealing NES288-294 at 28°C.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of interaction between T179A and NES288-294 mutations.

claim: The T179D nuclear translocation effect at 20°C was abolished in a T179D; NLS71-78 double mutant.
source: The T179D nuclear translocation effect at 20°C was abolished in a T179D; NLS71-78 double mutant (Figure 3D, significant interaction effect).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: T179D phosphomimic mutation promotes NLS71-78-dependent CMK-1 nuclear entry.
source: Therefore, T179D phosphomimic mutation promotes NLS71-78-dependent CMK-1 nuclear entry.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D and NLS71-78 interactions.

claim: Multiple calcium-dependent events in the cytoplasm converge on CMK-1 NLS71-78 element to activate its nuclear import upon prolonged cell activation.
source: Taken together with our previous finding (Ippolito et al., 2021), our new results suggest a model in which multiple calcium-dependent events in the cytoplasm converge on CMK-1 NLS71-78 element to activate its nuclear import upon prolonged cell activation (see cytoplasmic green arrows in Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: CMK-1(T179D) mutant protein at 28°C was not more nuclear than CMK-1(wt), but actually significantly more cytoplasmic.
source: In strong contrast to this prediction, CMK-1(T179D) mutant protein at 28°C was not more nuclear than CMK-1(wt), but actually significantly more cytoplasmic with a ratio similar to that of CMK-1(T179D) at 20°C (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The impact of T179D mutation is context-dependent.
source: Therefore, the impact of T179D mutation is context-dependent, and, in addition to its nuclear entry promoting effect revealed at 20°C, might also include an antagonistic nuclear export drive, which becomes apparent at 28°C to counteract the nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D at different temperatures.

claim: T179D mutation might include an antagonistic nuclear export drive, which becomes apparent at 28°C.
source: Therefore, the impact of T179D mutation is context-dependent, and, in addition to its nuclear entry promoting effect revealed at 20°C, might also include an antagonistic nuclear export drive, which becomes apparent at 28°C to counteract the nuclear accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D at different temperatures.

claim: The T179D-evoked cytoplasmic drive was strongly reduced in the absence of an intact NES288-294 element.
source: We found that the T179D-evoked cytoplasmic drive was strongly reduced in the absence of an intact NES288-294 element (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The T179D phospho-mimic mutation promotes CMK-1 nuclear export in a NES288-294-dependent manner.
source: We conclude that the T179D phospho-mimic mutation promotes CMK-1 nuclear export in a NES288-294-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on T179D and NES288-294 interactions.

claim: Prolonged FLP stimulation causes T179 phosphorylation, which activates both NLS71-78-dependent nuclear entry and NES288-294-dependent export pathways.
source: Taken together, our data suggest a model in which prolonged FLP stimulation causes T179 phosphorylation, which activates both NLS71-78-dependent nuclear entry (Figure 3G, cytoplasmic green arrow) and NES288-294-dependent export pathways (Figure 3G, nuclear green arrow).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: T179 phosphorylation results in an activated dynamic nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling.
source: T179 phosphorylation would thus result in (i) an activated dynamic nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling and (ii) a shift in CMK-1 equilibrium toward the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: T179 phosphorylation results in a shift in CMK-1 equilibrium toward the nucleus.
source: T179 phosphorylation would thus result in (i) an activated dynamic nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling and (ii) a shift in CMK-1 equilibrium toward the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: The shift in CMK-1 equilibrium toward the nucleus results from a synergy between the direct impact of T179 phosphorylation and the Ca2+/CaM-binding-evoked importin affinity increase, converging on NLS71-78.
source: The latter effect most likely results from a synergy between the direct impact of T179 phosphorylation and the Ca2+/CaM-binding-evoked importin affinity increase, converging on NLS71-78 in order for this pathway to dominate over the antagonistic pathways into play.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: In rats, CaM kinase kinase alpha is expressed in the nucleus.
source: In rats, CaM kinase kinase alpha is expressed in the nucleus, whereas CaM kinase kinase beta is expressed in the nucleus and/or the cytoplasm depending on the tissue (Kitani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kitani et al., 2003.

claim: In rats, CaM kinase kinase beta is expressed in the nucleus and/or the cytoplasm depending on the tissue.
source: In rats, CaM kinase kinase alpha is expressed in the nucleus, whereas CaM kinase kinase beta is expressed in the nucleus and/or the cytoplasm depending on the tissue (Kitani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kitani et al., 2003.

claim: The worm genome encodes two predicted CKK-1 isoforms (CKK-1a and CKK-1b), produced via alternative transcription start.
source: The worm genome encodes two predicted CKK-1 isoforms (CKK-1a and CKK-1b), produced via alternative transcription start (Figure 4A), which diverge in their N-terminal region.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CKK-1a and CKK-1b isoforms diverge in their N-terminal region.
source: The worm genome encodes two predicted CKK-1 isoforms (CKK-1a and CKK-1b), produced via alternative transcription start (Figure 4A), which diverge in their N-terminal region.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both CKK-1a and CKK-1b isoforms were markedly enriched in the cytoplasm.
source: Both isoforms were markedly enriched in the cytoplasm, with ratios similar to that of CMK-1 at rest (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: CKK-1 localization was not altered upon heat stimulation at 28°C for 90 min.
source: Furthermore, their localization was not altered upon heat stimulation at 28°C for 90 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Most of CKK-1 activity in FLP is likely to occur in the cytoplasm.
source: These data suggest that most of CKK-1 activity in FLP is likely to occur in the cytoplasm and that CMK-1 phosphorylation might therefore primarily take place in this compartment (as depicted in Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data of CKK-1.

claim: CMK-1 phosphorylation might primarily take place in the cytoplasm.
source: These data suggest that most of CKK-1 activity in FLP is likely to occur in the cytoplasm and that CMK-1 phosphorylation might therefore primarily take place in this compartment (as depicted in Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data of CKK-1.

claim: CMK-1 subcellular localization contributes to adjust sensory neuron activity according to past experience.
source: CMK-1 subcellular localization contributes to adjust sensory neuron activity according to past experience.
evidence: This is established from previous studies and the current work.

claim: Heat-evoked CMK-1 nuclear entry in FLP thermo-nociceptor neurons causes a decrease in the animal responsiveness to noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Heat-evoked CMK-1 nuclear entry in FLP thermo-nociceptor neurons causes a decrease in the animal responsiveness to noxious thermal stimuli (Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schild et al., 2014.

claim: The dual regulatory role of T179 phosphorylation in promoting bidirectional CMK-1 translocation across the nuclear envelope could be at the origin of cell stimulation-dependent CMK-1 shuttling cycles.
source: We speculate that the dual regulatory role of T179 phosphorylation in promoting bidirectional CMK-1 translocation across the nuclear envelope could be at the origin of cell stimulation-dependent CMK-1 shuttling cycles.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: A dynamic nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling might contribute to ensure that the T179 phosphorylation status of CMK-1 is frequently 'refreshed'.
source: Considering the cytoplasmic localization of CKK-1, we propose that a dynamic nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling might contribute to ensure that the T179 phosphorylation status of CMK-1 is frequently 'refreshed', in order for the nuclear pool of CMK-1 to reflect the current activation status of CKK-1 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: The whole process is likely to be also influenced by the activity of phosphatase(s) responsible for CMK-1 dephosphorylation on T179.
source: Furthermore, the whole process is likely to be also influenced by the activity of phosphatase(s) responsible for CMK-1 dephosphorylation on T179.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about additional regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Previous studies have reported transient, persistent, or sometimes no CMK-1 nuclear translocation in different neurons subjected to different stimulation regimens.
source: Previous studies have reported transient, persistent, or sometimes no CMK-1 nuclear translocation in different neurons subjected to different stimulation regimens (Ippolito et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2018; Moss et al., 2016; Schild et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The network of intrinsic regulatory elements might be the target of multiple intracellular signaling events to fine-tune CMK-1 localization in a variety of contexts.
source: We propose that the network of intrinsic regulatory elements that we have identified might be the target of multiple intracellular signaling events in order to fine-tune CMK-1 localization in a variety of contexts.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about broader implications.

claim: CaM binding and T179 phosphorylation converging on NLS71-78 and the antagonistic NES288-294-dependent export constitutes the primary mechanism explaining the CMK-1 equilibrium shift upon prolonged stimulation in FLP.
source: While CaM binding and T179 phosphorylation converging on NLS71-78 and the antagonistic NES288-294-dependent export constitutes the primary mechanism explaining the CMK-1 equilibrium shift upon prolonged stimulation in FLP (Figure 3G), the other elements could be more relevant in different contexts.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and presented as a model.

claim: NLS297-307 overlaps with the CaM-binding site.
source: The fact that NLS297-307 overlaps with the CaM-binding site and the fact that S325 phosphorylation status affects its NES activity represent additional regulation opportunities, which could be engaged in different cells or situations.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of CMK-1.

claim: S325 phosphorylation status affects its NES activity.
source: The fact that NLS297-307 overlaps with the CaM-binding site and the fact that S325 phosphorylation status affects its NES activity represent additional regulation opportunities, which could be engaged in different cells or situations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on S325 mutations.

claim: The expression of CMK-1 is much broader than that of CKK-1.
source: Indeed, based on previous reporter analyses and single-cell RNA seq data, the expression of CMK-1 is much broader than that of CKK-1 (Kimura et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimura et al., 2002 and Taylor et al., 2021.

claim: The activity of CaM kinase kinase in mammals was shown to be regulated by post-translational modifications.
source: The activity of CaM kinase kinase in mammals was also shown to be regulated by post-translational modifications (Green et al., 2011; Nakanishi et al., 2017; Takabatake et al., 2019) and this pathway may be silenced in specific situations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Green et al., 2011; Nakanishi et al., 2017; Takabatake et al., 2019.

claim: CaM kinases can couple cell activation with physiological changes taking place over relatively long timescales.
source: Being downstream effectors of intracellular calcium signaling, CaM kinases can couple cell activation with physiological changes taking place over relatively long timescales.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaM kinases.

claim: CaM kinase activity can be regulated by other signaling pathways.
source: Furthermore, multiple studies have shown that their kinase activity can be regulated by other signaling pathways (see Swulius and Waxham, 2008; Tokumitsu and Sakagami, 2022 for reviews), placing them as a hub for integrating multiple inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: CaM kinases serve as a hub for integrating multiple inputs.
source: Furthermore, multiple studies have shown that their kinase activity can be regulated by other signaling pathways (see Swulius and Waxham, 2008; Tokumitsu and Sakagami, 2022 for reviews), placing them as a hub for integrating multiple inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited reviews.

claim: Not only CaM kinase activity, but also the regulation of its subcellular localization are important targets of convergent regulatory inputs.
source: Our study supports the notion that not only CaM kinase activity, but also the regulation of its subcellular localization are important targets of convergent regulatory inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings of this study.

claim: Similar mechanisms might be relevant for CaM kinase regulation in different species and for different sensory modalities beyond thermo-nociceptive functions.
source: Owing to the large conservation of calcium signaling during evolution and in particular of the CaM kinase structural and functional architectures, similar mechanisms might be relevant for their regulation in different species and for different sensory modalities beyond thermo-nociceptive functions.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about broader evolutionary implications.
